title: Civic life starts close to home and leads to the ballot box
summary: Democracy works best when every voice is heard.
body_markdown:
### Check. Recheck. Vote.


Lisa Reppell, senior program manager for information literacy, knew she had found her path when she attended her first community town hall in 2001. Held at a Boise public library, the discussion centered on the Patriot Act and the tensions between civil liberties and national security. “Those are two deeply important values that require debate in the public square,” she recalls. She now leads information literacy on the Elections and Societal Resilience Team at Microsoft—and that includes AI, increasingly a front door to election information.


Reppell’s team is preparing to launch a voter education initiative ahead of the midterms:[Check. Recheck. Vote.](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/corporate-responsibility/elections) Originally launched in 2024 to help voters recognize risks posed by deepfakes, or deceptive AI-generated content, this year’s campaign focuses on practical AI literacy. She says, “We’re really trying to respond to the reality that AI is starting to change the way that people are finding information about the election—whether people are going to an AI chatbot or doing their same old internet search but with an AI-generated summary.”


Check. Recheck. Vote. encourages voters to check sources and citations behind an AI-generated answer, recheck by visiting those sources and comparing what other credible sources say, and vote using official information. Reppell is encouraged to see that more voters are using AI to deliberately understand the candidates and issues on their ballots. “AI can clarify information and compare the data sources you bring to it, but it shouldn’t tell you who to vote for,” she says. “AI can’t make your judgments for you.”
